entities.summary:
Luke (Lukáš) of Prague was a bishop of the Unitas Fratrum, one of the most significant theologians of the Bohemian Reformation. A key figure in the 16th-century religious upheaval that reshaped the spiritual landscape of Europe, Luke's teachings on the importance of personal faith and the authority of Scripture helped to fuel the flames of dissent among Protestant reformers. As the leader of the Unitas Fratrum, a movement that sought to reconcile Catholic and Protestant traditions, Luke played a crucial role in mediating the complex relationships between Catholics and Protestants during this tumultuous period in European history.

Born in 1486 in Prague, Bohemia (now the Czech Republic), Luke was raised in a devoutly Catholic family but later converted to Lutheranism. He studied theology at Charles University in Prague and was ordained as a priest in 1515. In 1517, Luke became the bishop of the Unitas Fratrum, a position he held until his death in 1528.

Luke's theological views were heavily influenced by the teachings of Martin Luther, but he also drew on the traditions of the Eastern Orthodox Church and the Czech mystics. His writings on the importance of personal faith and the authority of Scripture helped to shape the theological agenda of the Bohemian Reformation. In 1526, Luke traveled to the Council of Trent, where he engaged in debates with Catholic theologians and helped to shape the reform movement's stance on key issues such as baptism and the Eucharist.

Despite his significant contributions to the theological debates of his time, Luke's legacy was largely overshadowed by that of Martin Luther. However, his influence can be seen in the development of the Unitas Fratrum, which continued to play a major role in shaping the spiritual landscape of Europe during the 16th and 17th centuries.
